title: CARABULEA v. ROMANIA
summary: In Carabulea v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Carabulea, a Romanian national of Roma origin, brought a case against the Romanian state concerning the death of his brother, Gabriel Carabulea, while in police custody. The case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to ill-treatment and inadequate protection by law enforcement, particularly in situations involving deprivation of liberty. On 13 April 1996, Gabriel Carabulea was arrested in Bucharest by police officers, initially for alleged robbery and possession of counterfeit currency. After his arrest, he was detained in a police lock-up, where he reportedly appeared in good health. However, within days, Gabriel’s health deteriorated rapidly; he complained of pain and weakness, was transferred between several hospitals, and ultimately died on 16 April 1996. The applicant alleged that his brother’s death resulted from police ill-treatment and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of torture), 6 (right to a fair trial), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, declaring the application admissible. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent risks faced by Roma and Travellers in police custody and the importance of thorough, impartial investigations into deaths in detention, reflecting broader concerns about systemic discrimination in post-communist Europe.
